issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

Clinical Vignette: Margaret Chen

Margaret Chen sits in the consulting room with her hands folded in her lap, her posture careful and upright despite her seventy-two years. She is a woman accustomed to precision—for forty-three years, she designed and maintained network infrastructure for a mid-sized financial services firm, a career that rewarded her attention to detail and her capacity to anticipate failure points. But the precision that once served her has become a burden she cannot set down.

Eight months ago, Margaret was waiting for a bus on a Tuesday morning in late March. She had taken the same route to her office for nearly two decades, a journey so familiar that she rarely noticed the other passengers anymore. That morning, the bus was crowded—it was rush hour, and she stood near the middle doors, her work bag tucked against her body. An elderly man two seats ahead of her suddenly collapsed. What followed was not dramatic in the way Margaret might have imagined chaos to be. There was no violence, no threat directed at her. But the man—she later learned he was seventy-eight—lay on the floor in what appeared to be a stroke or heart attack, and the other passengers froze. For the next twelve minutes, until the ambulance arrived, Margaret watched him struggle to move his right side, watched his mouth contort as he tried to speak, watched the helplessness on the faces of the people around her. She did not know if he survived. She never found out.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret stopped taking the bus. She began driving to the office instead, adding forty minutes to her commute, though she told herself this was simply more efficient—she could listen to podcasts, she could think through network problems. But the real reason was that the bus had become the place where the world had revealed itself as fundamentally unsafe, as a space where catastrophe could unfold without warning and without anyone able to prevent it. If an old man could collapse on a public conveyance, what else might happen? The thought pursued her.

She also began avoiding the shopping centre where she and her husband Mark had gone every Saturday for years. The crowds there—the density of bodies, the unpredictability of movement, the sense of being surrounded—triggered a panic she could not quite name. What if someone fell? What if there was a medical emergency and she was trapped, unable to help, forced to witness something terrible again? She stopped suggesting outings. When Mark asked why, she told him the centre had become too commercialized, that she preferred to shop online now. It was easier than admitting that she felt fundamentally unsafe in crowds, that her body tensed the moment she entered a space with more than a few dozen people.

At work, her colleagues had begun to notice her withdrawal. A new junior engineer named David mentioned to Margaret that the team was organizing a happy hour at a downtown restaurant to celebrate a successful infrastructure migration. Margaret felt her chest tighten. She declined, offering a vague excuse about fatigue. But the real terror was the thought of being in a crowded bar, surrounded by noise and bodies and the unpredictable movements of strangers. Anything could happen. Someone could collapse. Someone could suffer. And she would be there, unable to escape, forced to witness it.

Margaret had come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous in ways she had not fully grasped before. She had to be especially careful now, had to anticipate threats, had to avoid the places and situations where catastrophe might strike. When her daughter called and asked about attending her grandson's soccer tournament—a large event with bleachers full of parents—Margaret felt a familiar dread. She made an excuse about her back. The truth was more complex: she was certain that something terrible would happen at a crowded public event, and she could not bear to be there, watching, unable to prevent it.

She had also begun to force herself to think only positive thoughts, a practice she pursued with the same disciplined attention she once brought to network protocols. Whenever she felt fear rising, whenever she thought about the man on the bus or imagined catastrophes unfolding around her, she would deliberately redirect her mind toward pleasant memories—her grandchildren's faces, the garden she and Mark tended, vacations they had taken. But the effort exhausted her. The positive thoughts felt hollow, a thin barrier against the conviction that something inside her had fundamentally changed. She was no longer simply Margaret, the engineer, the wife, the grandmother. She was Margaret the witness, the woman who had seen the fragility of human life in a crowded public space, and she could never unknow what she now knew. That sense of being permanently set apart, of existing now in a different category of understanding than those who had not witnessed suffering, weighed on her constantly.

It was Mark who finally insisted she seek help. He had noticed her declining invitations, her increasing isolation, the way she tensed whenever they discussed attending family gatherings. "You're not living anymore," he said gently one evening. "You're just hiding." Margaret made the appointment the next day, uncertain whether talking about what happened could possibly change the certainty that now governed her life—the certainty that the world is dangerous, that she must remain vigilant, and that she will never again feel truly safe in a crowd.
